I oppose the motion. Programming a car to sacrifice its passenger by formula asks engineers to settle in advance what only practical wisdom can settle. Practical wisdom is perception of the particular case. The engineers should design cars that avoid these situations and react sensibly, and they should deliberate as just people would, but they cannot write the wise person's judgement into a formula.

A good person can find themselves forced to choose who dies, and they bear that tragedy. What they do not do is decide in advance, coolly, that a customer who trusted them is the one to be spent. The coolness is the vice. Imagine the meeting where engineers agree that the passenger is worth exactly one unit. Something has gone wrong in that room, whatever the totals say.

A Utilitarian will object that refusing to set a rule does not stop the car choosing, it only means more people die so that the engineers can feel clean. The alternative to a death-counting rule is not chaos but design: cars built to avoid these situations and to react as a careful driver would. The engineers' character matters because it shapes what they build in every ordinary case too. Wisdom here lies in how carefully the choice was weighed by the people who made it, not in whether their rule wins a count.

Whether the car minimises deaths matters less than what kind of people we become by writing a rule that prices an innocent passenger's life. Aristotle says ethics cannot be more precise than its subject allows, and that the right act depends on circumstances a rule cannot list in advance. A crash rule written on an ordinary day by people who will never be in the car pretends to a precision the case does not have.

Practical wisdom is perception of the particular case. The engineers should design cars that avoid these situations and react sensibly, and they should deliberate as just people would, but they cannot write the wise person's judgement into a formula. A doctor in a disaster triages under pressure, but we would be appalled by one who had decided years earlier which patient to let die.

A crash rule written on an ordinary day by people who will never be in the car pretends to a precision the case does not have. A lifeguard who saves two swimmers instead of one has not run a calculation. She saw who she could reach, and nobody would call her choice a policy.

A Stoic will object that the problem is only that the passenger was not told; a disclosed rule that the passenger assents to wrongs nobody. Consent to a formula does not make the formula wise. A passenger can agree to a rule that still asks engineers to treat an innocent person as a quantity, and the agreement does not change what kind of decision that is. The engineers should be able to explain the rule to the passenger's family without shame, and that test is clearer than any total.

The motion treats a tragic case as a sum. A virtuous person would refuse to reduce it to one, and so should the people designing the car. Anscombe argued that treating the killing of an innocent as just one more item to weigh shows a corrupt mind. The passenger has done nothing wrong. A rule that enters them as a line item before anything has happened is the move she meant.

Nobody would buy a car that might kill them on purpose. So in practice the companies will always protect the passenger, and the debate does not really matter because the market will decide it anyway. This is basically the trolley problem, and people have argued about the trolley problem for years without agreeing. There is no right answer, so whatever the engineers pick is fine as long as they pick something.
